prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can’t get rid of useful things and nobody wants to pick them up, I keep forgetting where I lay my umbrella. I don’t leave footprints in the snow anymore, we haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long I wonder if I still got it. Because once I had it. I heard about a boy who once tied a string to his brother, he tied his brother to the ocean and the ocean to the blackbird— from the ground all the birds look like blackbirds from the ground a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The aliens are coming, they walk through birthday parties and basically go unnoticed. And this is kind of how I go through life, once I heated up a spoon in the microwave the fish have so much mercury in them they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her her neck explodes with a million little spiders. Meanwhile in a forest somewhere someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks something is coming soon I keep a bucket of lambs blood by the front door.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores anxiety, dispossession, forgotten histories of violence, and apocalyptic dread through surreal, associative imagery and fragmented personal confession. It suggests that ordinary life is haunted by war, decay, and inherited trauma, making the speaker’s private unease feel like a symptom of broader cultural collapse.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Stealth, Bomber

outputs.L1:
I can’t bring myself to get rid of useful things, and no one wants to come pick them up. I keep forgetting where I’ve left my umbrella. I no longer leave footprints in the snow. We haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long that I wonder whether I still have it in me—because once, I did.

I heard about a boy who once tied a string to his brother; he tied his brother to the ocean, and the ocean to the blackbird. From the ground, all birds look like blackbirds. From the ground, a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The aliens are coming; they walk through birthday parties and, for the most part, go unnoticed.

And this is more or less how I move through life. Once, I heated a spoon in the microwave. The fish have so much mercury in them that they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her, her neck explodes with a million little spiders.

Meanwhile, in a forest somewhere, someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks. Something is coming soon. I keep a bucket of lamb’s blood by the front door.
outputs.L2:
I can’t bring myself to throw away objects that still have a purpose, and no one will come take them off my hands. I’m always misplacing my umbrella. My feet no longer mark the snow. It’s been such a long time since a war was fought here at home that I’m not sure I’d know what to do anymore—though there was a time when I did.

I once heard a story about a boy who fastened a cord to his brother, then bound his brother to the sea, and the sea to a blackbird. Seen from below, every bird seems like a blackbird; seen from below, a Stealth Bomber resembles a spacecraft. The extraterrestrials are on their way, moving through birthday celebrations without anyone really noticing them.

That is more or less the way I pass through the world. Once, I put a spoon in the microwave to warm it. Fish contain so much mercury now that they give off sparks. Someone placed in my hands a Civil War bayonet and a copper penny eaten away by rust. When workers dismantle the Statue of Liberty to wash her, a million tiny spiders burst from her throat.

At the same time, in some forest, someone sliced open my grandmother’s stomach and packed it with bricks. Something is about to arrive. I keep a pail of lamb’s blood beside the front entrance.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents themselves as someone who has difficulty letting go of useful objects, even when those objects may no longer be necessary. This tendency is paired with a more ordinary kind of disorientation: they repeatedly misplace everyday things, such as an umbrella. These details suggest a mind preoccupied with both practical survival and emotional attachment, unable to fully trust that what is needed will be available when it is needed.

The text also reflects on the speaker’s distance from war. Although they are not directly in a battlefield, war remains present as a pressure on the imagination. The speaker questions whether they still possess an older capacity for violence, endurance, or survival—qualities that may once have felt necessary in more dangerous conditions. This uncertainty creates a tension between the relative safety of ordinary life and the fear that such safety may be temporary or illusory.

Throughout the poem, the world appears surreal and unstable. Ordinary domestic life blends with threatening, strange images: aliens, bombers, fish filled with mercury, and weapons from history. These images make the familiar world feel contaminated by danger. The result is an atmosphere in which everyday reality cannot be separated from disaster, invasion, poisoning, and warfare.

The poem also links national symbols and historical memory with decay and fear. References to the Civil War and the Statue of Liberty do not appear as simple patriotic images; instead, they are surrounded by unsettling associations. The nation’s history and ideals seem haunted by violence, deterioration, and anxiety. Symbols that might normally represent freedom or unity become part of a darker landscape marked by conflict and unease.

By the end, the speaker’s anxiety has become a sense of impending threat. The final image of keeping a bucket of lamb’s blood by the door suggests a desperate, almost ritualistic form of protection. It evokes sacrifice, warning, and defense against an approaching danger. The poem closes not with resolution, but with the speaker preparing for something terrible that may soon arrive.
outputs.L4:
Anxiety arrives first as a small domestic disturbance: a glass left trembling on the edge of the sink, a stain spreading on the ceiling, the faint smell of smoke in a room where nothing is burning. It does not announce itself as terror. It appears in the ordinary places, in the hallway, in the supermarket aisle, in the pause before sleep, and it makes the familiar world look staged and unstable. The speaker moves through daily life as though through a house built over ruins, aware that beneath every gesture there is something buried, something unacknowledged and restless.

The text unfolds through surreal and associative images rather than through a clear narrative. Memories, dreams, historical fragments, and private fears blur together. A cracked plate becomes a battlefield. A family photograph becomes evidence. A streetlight flickers like a warning signal from some abandoned century. The speaker’s mind does not move in a straight line; it circles, leaps, repeats, and interrupts itself. This fragmentation suggests a consciousness under pressure, unable to separate personal unease from the larger violence that surrounds and precedes it.

Dispossession runs through the work as both material condition and emotional inheritance. There is a sense that homes have been taken, languages erased, graves neglected, and names misremembered or deliberately removed. The speaker feels surrounded by absences: people who should have been mentioned but were not, histories that should have been taught but were hidden, losses that have been converted into silence. The world appears full of objects that belong to someone else, or once did: land, furniture, jewelry, buildings, even stories. Nothing feels innocent because everything may have passed through hands marked by force.

The forgotten histories of violence are not truly forgotten; they return in distorted forms. They appear as nightmares, compulsions, rumors, bodily sensations, and sudden flashes of dread. The past is not past in this text. It leaks into the present like contaminated water. War is not confined to the battlefield, nor to the years in which it officially occurred. It survives in architecture, in borders, in family habits, in the way people avoid certain subjects at dinner. The speaker senses that the present has been built out of unresolved catastrophe, and that ordinary peace is only a thin covering stretched over older wounds.

This is why the imagery often feels apocalyptic. The apocalypse is not simply imagined as a future event, a final explosion or flood or burning sky. It is already underway, scattered across everyday life in signs of decay and exhaustion. Buildings rot. Animals behave strangely. Weather turns hostile. Machines hum with indifference. The body itself becomes an unreliable shelter, full of panic, illness, and inherited alarm. The speaker seems to live in a world after disaster and before disaster at the same time, suspended between what has already happened and what seems certain to come.

The personal confession at the center of the text is therefore unstable. When the speaker admits fear, shame, or dread, these feelings do not remain private. They expand outward, attaching themselves to history, politics, family, and landscape. The speaker’s anxiety becomes a kind of evidence, a symptom of a wider collapse. Their inner life registers pressures that the culture would prefer to deny. Panic is not presented as irrational, but as a form of perception: a response to living among ruins while being told that everything is normal.

Ordinary life, in this vision, is haunted. A morning commute contains the echo of forced marches. A neighborhood development stands over the memory of eviction. The comfort of a warm room depends on systems of extraction and forgetting. Even intimate moments are shadowed by violence that has been inherited rather than chosen. The speaker cannot look at the world without seeing what has been covered over, and cannot look inward without finding traces of that same world embedded in the self.

The result is a text of dread, but also of recognition. Its fragmented, surreal style mirrors the difficulty of confronting histories that have been denied or broken apart. It refuses the comfort of a single explanation. Instead, it presents anxiety as something both personal and collective, both psychological and historical. The speaker’s unease is not merely an individual disorder; it is the emotional weather of a culture built on dispossession, denial, and decay. In this way, the text suggests that to feel haunted may be an honest response to a haunted world.

Because modern warfare often depends on surprise and precision, the stealth bomber has become one of the most advanced aircraft ever developed. Its unique design helps it avoid radar detection, allowing it to fly deep into enemy territory with a much lower chance of being seen. Unlike traditional bombers, a stealth bomber is built with special materials, angled surfaces, and advanced technology that reduce its radar signature.

The main purpose of a stealth bomber is to deliver powerful strikes while remaining hidden for as long as possible. Because it can travel long distances and carry a wide range of weapons, it plays an important role in strategic military operations. These aircraft are often used when a mission requires secrecy, accuracy, and the ability to reach heavily defended targets.

A stealth bomber is not only a symbol of military strength but also a result of decades of engineering and innovation. Its development shows how technology can change the way conflicts are fought. Because staying undetected can make the difference between success and failure, stealth remains one of the most valuable features in modern aviation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the first person about paranoia, memory, useless objects, American history, aliens, and a sense that something terrible is approaching.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep a drawer for the useless things: a brass key that opens no republic, a wristwatch stopped at the hour of my birth, three pennies green with the weather of other pockets, a motel Bible with all the begats underlined by a stranger’s panic. At night the drawer knocks from the inside like a little coffin. I tell myself it is only the house settling, but the house is not old enough to know how to settle. It was built on a battlefield, or a cornfield, or an Indian burial ground, or a parking lot where no one can remember what was paved over first.

My memory has been acting federal. It redacts the faces of my mother and leaves only her apron, floating in the kitchen like a flag after the war. It classifies my childhood under the heading of national security. Sometimes I recall a parade: drums, horses, the moon caught in the bell of a tuba. Sometimes I recall the same parade ending with all the spectators turning toward me in perfect silence, their mouths full of moths.

I was taught American history as a sequence of furniture: the Mayflower was a table; the Constitution, a chair no one could sit in without becoming taller; the Civil War, a bed split down the middle by a sword; the moon landing, a television glowing in a room where my father slept with his boots on. George Washington’s wooden teeth chatter in my cupboard. Lincoln stands in my hallway at three in the morning, not a ghost but a warning label, his tall hat full of black rain. The presidents whisper through the plumbing, counting backward from the future.

I have seen the aliens only in reflections: in the dark window above the sink, in the spoon before soup, in the blank eye of the unplugged television. They are pale and patient, with the posture of librarians. They do not abduct me. They inventory me. They measure the distance between my fear and my name. One of them wears my grandfather’s face, or perhaps my grandfather wore its face all along, through the Depression, through Korea, through every Thanksgiving where he carved the turkey as if opening a sealed message from space.

Every object I own has become a witness. The umbrella accuses me of drought. The broken radio mutters crop reports from 1933. A porcelain dog stares at the door with such devotion that I no longer trust the door. Even the dust arranges itself into maps of states I have never visited, borders trembling, capitals marked by tiny black teeth.

Something is coming. I know because the birds have begun flying in the shape of questions. I know because the neighbors bring in their flags at sunset and the flags come back out by themselves at dawn, stiff and bright, smelling of electricity. I know because my dreams now arrive in sealed envelopes stamped RETURN TO SENDER, and inside each one is a photograph of the ocean standing upright at the end of the street.

I walk through my rooms touching everything I cannot use. The key, the watch, the pennies, the Bible, the spoon, the dog. I touch them like relics, like buttons in a cockpit, like bones in the hand of a saint. If I remember correctly, the country was founded by men afraid of kings and haunted by weather. If I remember incorrectly, it was founded by aliens who mistook our loneliness for intelligence.

Outside, the sirens practice their long vowel. The sky lowers its enormous blue ear to the roof. I press my own ear to the drawer and hear the small things inside arranging themselves for departure. I want to say I am ready. I want to say I have always been ready. But my mouth is full of moths, and the terrible thing is almost here, wearing history like a mask, wearing my memory like a coat, knocking politely, patiently, uselessly, at every door in America.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange, associative monologue in the style of contemporary experimental poetry, with images of umbrellas, snow, war, blackbirds, stealth bombers, the Statue of Liberty, and lamb’s blood.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep opening the umbrella indoors  
as if weather were a confession  
and the ceiling, embarrassed, begins to snow.

White static on the table.  
White ash in the spoon.  
White maps folded into the mouths of generals  
who dream in grid coordinates and wake  
with blackbirds nesting in their helmets.

Listen: the sky is practicing its disappearance.

A stealth bomber passes overhead  
like a thought no one admits to having—  
all angles, no apology,  
a cathedral made of refusal.  
Beneath it, children draw the sun  
with too many teeth.

The Statue of Liberty stands ankle-deep  
in gray water, holding up her tired flame  
like a match at the end of history.  
Her robe smells of salt, diesel, wet wool.  
Someone has tied umbrellas to her crown  
and each one turns inside out  
in the patriotic wind.

Snow falls on the checkpoints.  
Snow falls on the parade.  
Snow falls on the lamb’s blood drying  
in a blue enamel bowl,  
where a mother has dipped her fingers  
to mark the door, the door, the door—  
as if repetition could save us,  
as if the angel of ruin were literate.

I have carried a blackbird in my coat for years.  
It does not sing.  
It clicks like a detonator.  
It watches the news through my ribs  
and names every country by its wound.

Somewhere, umbrellas bloom in a field  
after the shelling,  
small black flowers with metal stems,  
sheltering nothing.  
Snow gathers in their inverted cups.  
The soldiers call it peace  
because it is quiet enough  
to hear the blood moving.

And Liberty, green with weather,  
green with waiting,  
raises her torch to inspect the clouds—  
but the clouds are aircraft,  
and the aircraft are prayers,  
and the prayers are falling open  
like broken umbrellas over the city.

I say lamb and mean innocence.  
I say blood and mean border.  
I say snow and mean forgetting,  
but the blackbirds refuse it.  
They land on the white ground  
like punctuation from a burned book,  
comma, comma, comma,  
until the whole field becomes a sentence  
we are afraid to finish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark absurdist paragraph that feels like someone spiraling through disconnected memories and conspiracy-like thoughts, mixing domestic details with violent historical imagery.
counterfactuals.output: The kettle clicks off like a tiny government collapsing, and suddenly I’m remembering the stain under the sink, the one shaped like a cavalry charge, or maybe a map of countries invented by men with fevers and medals. Mother used to fold towels as if preparing flags for surrender, while the radio hissed about weather fronts, sugar prices, secret tunnels beneath the post office, the moon being hollow and full of bureaucrats. I butter my toast and think of trenches filling with rain, of emperors misplacing whole villages in the pockets of their coats, of a pigeon wearing a wire. The refrigerator hums in code. The cat stares at the cupboard where we keep the batteries, and I know she knows about the committee, the one that meets behind the wallpaper and replaces our spoons with slightly heavier spoons. Outside, the neighbor trims his roses with the calm of a dictator signing forms, petals falling like tiny red uniforms, and somewhere in my memory a school bell rings over smoke, over boots, over the soft domestic terror of a table set for people who are never coming home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness prose poem with no clear plot, full of uncanny metaphors, childhood rumors, military objects, polluted fish, family horror, and apocalyptic dread.
counterfactuals.output:
In the attic the toy soldiers keep changing wars.

Mother says don’t touch them, they belonged to someone with a fever, someone who came home with his pockets full of black buttons and no shadow. Father says all metal remembers the shape of a wound. My brother put a bayonet under his pillow once and dreamed his teeth were marching out of his mouth in little helmets.

When we were children there was a rumor that the pond behind the school had no bottom. Then it had a bottom but the bottom was made of drowned bicycles. Then it was full of catfish with human hands. Then the factory upstream coughed up a rainbow slick and the fish began floating to the surface with their eyes milky and accusatory, their bellies printed with oil, their mouths opening and closing like they were trying to say our names in the language before language.

We poked them with sticks. We were innocent, which is to say we were practicing.

All summer the neighborhood smelled like pennies and wet fur. The old women on the porches whispered that if you looked into the storm drain at dusk you could see the future: a room with no doors, a crib full of ash, a wedding cake crawling with ants, the moon lowered into the street like a dead cow. Nobody looked except me. I saw my grandmother’s hands folding a flag that was also a baby blanket, folding and folding until there was nothing left but a hard blue triangle and one bright star blinking like an eye in a socket.

The television spoke in emergency tones. The radio spoke in numbers. The sky had the color of dishwater after knives.

In the garage Father kept a gas mask in a cardboard box beside the Christmas ornaments. It had round glass eyes and a rubber snout, and I believed it was an animal we had trapped and starved. Once I wore it and my own breathing became a stranger dragging furniture across an empty house. My sister cried because she said I looked like the doctor from her nightmare, the one who lived inside the wall and measured children for their coffins with a red ribbon.

There were always measurements. Height marked on the kitchen doorframe. Rainfall in a dented can. Radiation in cartoons. How much flour left. How much battery left. How far to the shelter. How long a person can hold their breath underwater, under rubble, under a table while adults scream in the next room and the ceiling fan turns slowly like a helicopter deciding where to land.

At night the curtains ballooned inward, though the windows were closed.

The house had its own weather. Mold bloomed in the corners like dark intelligence. The basement pipes knocked out messages from the country of the dead. Aunt Lydia said our bloodline was cursed because great-grandfather stole a ring from a corpse, but Uncle Ray said no, it was because of the mine, the layoffs, the drinking, the war, the thing in men that keeps digging after the earth has already begun to bleed.

Nobody ever agreed on the curse, only that it had a name somewhere.

My cousin found a mortar shell in the weeds by the old training ground and brought it home like a trophy. The adults turned pale in the special way adults turn pale when childhood reaches into history and pulls out something live. We stood in the driveway while a man in uniform carried it away with both hands, tender as a priest. For weeks afterward I imagined it sleeping beneath his truck seat, dreaming of fire, dreaming of all our houses opening like flowers.

The creek behind the slaughterhouse ran green in March, silver in June, red whenever no one admitted anything. Fish came up crooked there, spines bent like question marks, fins ragged as burned paper. We called them Jesus fish because they floated on their sides and would not stay buried. Bury one in the mud and by morning it returned to the bank, wearing a necklace of flies.

Someone said they had eaten the waste from the plant.
Someone said they had eaten a missing boy.
Someone said the government was putting things in the water to make us obedient.
Someone said obedience was what water had always wanted from us.

I remember my mother washing dishes with her back turned, shoulders sharp beneath her housedress, whispering not prayers exactly but inventories: bleach, salt, matches, canned peaches, iodine, bullets. I remember my father asleep at the table, one hand curled around an empty glass, the other resting on the family Bible as if keeping something inside it from getting out. I remember the baby monitor crackling though there was no baby anymore, only a small room painted yellow, only a crib disassembled in the closet, only my mother standing there sometimes with her arms bent around nothing, rocking nothing, humming to the air until the air seemed to gain weight.

The rumor was that babies could hear the end of the world before anyone else.

The rumor was that dogs could see it coming and that was why they barked at thunder.

The rumor was that if the sirens ever started, you should not look at the flash, but everyone wanted to know what color God would be when He finally made a mistake.

School taught us to crouch under desks as if wood could negotiate with fire. We pressed our faces to the gum-specked undersides and smelled pencil shavings, dust, the sour breath of generations. Our teacher wore a whistle around her neck. Her hands trembled when the jets passed over. She said it was only practice. Everything was only practice: the drills, the funerals, the way we learned to stop crying quietly, the way we watched men clean rifles on kitchen tables while cartoons laughed in the next room.

Sometimes I think childhood was just a long corridor lined with coats, and inside every coat was a soldier, and inside every soldier was a child trying not to breathe.

The clouds gathered like infected wool. Birds abandoned the telephone wires. The pond grew a skin. In the pantry, cans swelled with secret weather. My brother said he heard music coming from the electrical outlets. My sister said the wallpaper was blinking. Mother cut everyone’s hair short in the yard and burned the clippings in a coffee can because she said hair was evidence and evidence was how they found you.

Who they were changed from week to week.

Men in vans. Men in uniforms. Men underground. Men above the atmosphere. Men with clipboards. Men with faces like closed schools. Men who knew the real names of rivers and could call poison out of them like dogs.

The moon rusted. The sun bruised. The horizon made a low animal sound.

And still we ate dinner. Still we passed the salt. Still Father carved the meat with the ceremonial sadness of a nation splitting a body into portions. Still Mother smiled with all her teeth showing, not happiness but warning. Still the old gas mask watched from the shelf, its glass eyes fogged from within, as though something inside it had begun breathing before us.

Outside, the dead fish turned in the ditch, pale coins in the drainage of the empire.

Inside, the family portrait tilted one degree farther each year.

I keep thinking the end will arrive as a trumpet, a mushroom, a door of light, but maybe it has always been arriving as tap water, as lullaby, as mildew, as a toy soldier warmed in a child’s fist, as the rumor that becomes true only after everyone who repeated it is gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a creepy avant-garde literary passage from the perspective of a person who feels invisible and haunted by American symbols, aliens, dead relatives, and omens at the front door.
counterfactuals.output:
At the front door, the flag hangs without wind, stripes slack as butcher’s ribbons, stars dimmed by porchlight and insect dust. It is always there before I open, though I do not remember hanging it. I do not remember moving here. I do not remember becoming the kind of person a house can forget.

The bell rings with no hand on it.

Through the peephole: nothing. Then too much. A bald eagle perched on the welcome mat, head turned sideways, one yellow eye full of legal tender. A man in an astronaut suit standing behind it, visor black as a sealed oven. My grandmother in her burial dress, holding a casserole with both hands. The casserole is covered in foil. The foil is moving.

“Let us in,” says nobody.

I press my palm to the door. The wood is warm. Behind me, the television plays the anthem to a room of empty furniture. Rockets bloom over a stadium I have never visited. Men in uniforms salute until their fingers fuse to their brows. The crowd cheers in the language of static.

I have not appeared in a mirror for weeks.

At first I thought it was the lighting. Then grief. Then a clerical error in the universe. I stood before the bathroom glass and watched the towel rack, the cracked tile, the sink spotted with toothpaste, but not my face. I lifted my hand and the faucet lifted nothing. I opened my mouth and the medicine cabinet yawned back.

My dead uncle says this is normal.

He sits each night at the kitchen table, smoking the brand he quit in 1987. Ash collects in a neat gray pyramid on the placemat that says GOD BLESS AMERICA. He tells me the government has a drawer for people like me. He tells me the aliens came long before the pilgrims and wore them like gloves. He tells me my mother was right to cover mirrors during funerals, but wrong to uncover them afterward.

From the ceiling, a green light leaks.

It arrives around three in the morning, thin as a hospital wristband, and scans the hallway where my shadow should be. I hear little feet above the plaster. I hear instruments. I hear the dry click of photographs being taken of rooms I am not in. Once, a voice like a flute played backward whispered my Social Security number through the vent.

At the door, the bell rings again.

I do not answer. I have answered before.

The last time, there was a mailbox full of teeth. A baseball split down the seam, red stitches twitching like nerves. My father, twenty years dead, asking if I had seen his good shoes. Three small gray beings in campaign buttons stood under the porch awning, each holding a sparkler, each with my eyes.

They looked past me when I opened the door.

Everyone does.

The census taker looked through my shoulder and marked the house vacant. The neighbor’s dog barked at the space beside me, never at me. Children on bicycles swerved around my absence. At the grocery store, the automatic doors would not open until someone real came near.

Only the omens know where I live.

Tonight they gather: crow feather, cracked dime, milk gone sour before its date, a moth shaped like a tiny president beating itself against the porch bulb. The eagle scratches at the threshold. Grandmother hums from inside the foil. The astronaut raises one gloved hand and knocks, though the bell is still ringing.

I lean close to the peephole.

On the other side, America stands in the dark, enormous and hollow, wearing the faces of my relatives, wearing the moon as a badge, wearing the flag as skin. It has come to collect its missing citizen. It has brought witnesses from the stars.

“I’m not here,” I whisper.

The door whispers back, in my mother’s voice:

“That has never saved anyone.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
